'''Julie LaRoche''' is a Canadian marine biologist. She is a Tier 1 [[Canada Research Chair]] in Marine Microbial Genomics and Biogeochemistry at [[Dalhousie University]].

==Early life and education==
LaRoche was born in Quebec, Canada. She earned her [[Bachelor of Science]] from [[McGill University]] and her PhD in [[Biological oceanography|Biological Oceanography]] at [[Dalhousie University]].<ref name = "x">{{cite web |title=Prof. Dr. Julie LaRoche |url=http://www.laborundmore.com/research/9840/Prof.-Dr.-Julie-LaRoche.html |website=laborundmore.com |accessdate=December 3, 2019 |language=French}}</ref> While earning her PhD at Dalhouse, she met her future husband Douglas Wallace.<ref>{{cite web |last1=McNutt |first1=Ryan |title=OCEANS RESEARCH GETS A BOOST |url=https://www.dal.ca/news/2010/05/17/ocean.html |website=dal.ca |accessdate=December 3, 2019 |date=May 17, 2010}}</ref>

==Career==
After completing her postdoctoral studies at Dalhousie University, LaRoche conducted research at the [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]] (BNL).<ref name = "x"/> While there, LaRoche co-published “Flavodoxin expression as an indicator of iron limitation in marine diatoms" with [[Helen Murray-Tobin]] which earned them the [[Luigi Provasoli]] Award from the [[Phycological Society of America]] for the most outstanding research paper published in the Journal of Phycology.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Greenberg|first1=Diane|title=Oceanography Researchers Recognized |url=https://www.bnl.gov/bnlweb/pubaf/bulletin/1997/bb041897.pdf |website=bnl.gov |accessdate=December 3, 2019 |page=2 |date=April 18, 1997}}</ref> She also studied how stress affects phytoplankton.<ref>{{cite web |title=Iron Weighs Heavily In Ocean Plankton Growth, CO2 Absorption |url=https://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/1996-10/BNL-IWHI-091096.php |website=eurekalert.org |accessdate=December 3, 2019 |date=October 9, 1996}}</ref>  In 1998, LaRoche accepted a position at the University of Kiel as a professor in their Institute of Oceanography.<ref name ="x"/>

LaRoche and her husband stayed in Germany until 2010 when they both accepted placements at their alma mater, Dalhousie. LaRoche was appointed a Tier 1 [[Canada Research Chair]] in Marine Microbial Genomics and Biogeochemistry, and her husband was appointed the University's Canada Excellence Research Chair.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Weeren |first1=Marie |title=THE RIPPLE EFFECT |url=https://www.dal.ca/news/2010/06/29/wallace.html |website=dal.ca |accessdate=December 3, 2019 |date=June 30, 2010}}</ref> Upon her return, she developed a lab to research how global climate change is affecting marine microbes and biochemical processes.<ref>{{cite web |title=Monitoring Marine Microbes |url=https://www.bdbiosciences.com/ca/s/anewsinterlaroche |website=bdbiosciences.com |accessdate=December 3, 2019}}</ref> She specifically studied how phytoplankton and marine bacteria are affected by increases in temperature and decreases in pH.<ref>{{cite web |title=Deciphering the Role of the Invisible Marine Life with Julie LaRoche |url=https://www.ace-net.ca/portfolio_page/deciphering-the-role-of-the-invisible-marine-life/ |website=ace-net.ca |accessdate=December 3, 2019}}</ref> In 2016, she received $149,900 in funding for her plankton research project, which allowed her to purchase a holographic microscope for a commercial ship she uses to study the Deep Panuke drilling station.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Kennedy |first1=Grace |title=Dalhousie gets boost for plankton research |url=https://signalhfx.ca/dalhousie-gets-boost-for-plankton-research/ |website=signalhfx.ca |accessdate=December 3, 2019 |date=February 24, 2016}}</ref> Previously, her team had only been able to analyze sample of water twice a year until The Atlantic Canadian company voluntarily provided the lab with free access on the Atlantic Condor.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Comeau |first1=Nikki |title=A blooming partnership to advance ocean research |url=https://www.dal.ca/faculty/science/news-events/news/2016/02/19/a_blooming_partnership_to_advance_ocean_research.html |website=dal.ca |accessdate=December 3, 2019 |date=February 19, 2016}}</ref> The next year, she partnered with Canada C3, a 150-day expedition along the Atlantic, Arctic and Pacific coasts, to collect and share data.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Lewis |first1=Patti |title=BIOLOGIST SLEUTHS SOLVE MYSTERIES WITH DNA |url=https://www.dal.ca/news/2017/08/10/biologist-sleuths-solve-mysteries-with-dna.html |website=dal.ca |accessdate=December 3, 2019 |date=August 10, 2017}}</ref>

In 2019, LaRoche was renewed as a Canada Research Chair.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Charlton |first1=Michele |title=DALHOUSIE HOME TO SIX NEW CANADA RESEARCH CHAIRS |url=https://www.dal.ca/news/2019/07/03/dalhousie-home-to-six-new-canada-research-chairs.html |website=dal.ca |accessdate=December 3, 2019 |date=July 3, 2019}}</ref>

To date, LaRoche has published over 170 academic publications, which have been cited over 30,000 times, resulting in an [[h-index]] of 70.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Julie LaRoche |url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?view_op=list_works&hl=en&hl=en&user=UsVhHNMAAAAJ |access-date=2024-02-06 |website=scholar.google.com}}</ref>
